title: Multi-step paywalls: why they can convert better and how to test your own
summary: Multi-step paywalls convert 5.2% of sessions vs. 2.7% for single-screen. Walk through three proven UX patterns, 12+ real app examples, and how to test them.
body_markdown:
There’s nothing worse than sitting through a presentation and being confronted with a wall of text. We’ve all been there: six bullet points crammed onto a single slide, the text barely readable, and you’re left racing to take it all in before the presenter moves on. By the time they do, you don’t even remember bullet number one.


Paywalls face a similar challenge: we have an even smaller screen to work with, yet we still try to cram as much information as possible into it. The[State of Subscription Apps 2026 report](https://www.revenuecat.com/state-of-subscription-apps/) showed that most paywalls include:


- A highlighted price
- Multiple plan options
- A feature list
- Free trial messaging


And that’s just the beginning. It’s a lot to squeeze onto one screen, and the result can be much like that dreaded presentation slide: too much information, too little space, and eyes that slowly begin to glaze over. Worst of allNo, you can’t even reach for your phone to distract yourself… you’re already on it.


## Do multi-page paywalls convert better?


Ironically, the solution is simple. Just like with slides, **no one said everything has to fit on a single paywall** . A good presentation (in my opinion, at least) makes one key point per slide. A good paywall can do the same.


A multi-step paywall (also called multi-page, multi-screen, multi-stage paywall) is a sequence of screens that users move through by tapping a button, with the purchase taking place on the final screen.


And the data on multi-page paywalls is promising. While very few apps split their paywalls into multiple steps — based on RevenueCat’s data, less than 3% of apps are currently using multi-page paywalls — those that do are converting better:


- In the median app, **5.2% of multi-page paywall sessions lead to a trial or purchase** vs. 2.7% for a single-page paywall
- For apps using both types of paywall, a whopping **77% convert better with multi-page paywalls**


In[RevenueCat Paywalls](https://www.revenuecat.com/feature/paywalls) , you can add each screen as a ‘step’ (see[multi-step paywalls](https://www.revenuecat.com/docs/tools/paywalls/creating-paywalls#multi-step-paywalls) in Docs). That distinction matters because a step doesn’t always need to be a completely new page.


RevenueCat Paywalls Editor


I’ve always felt that the line between onboarding and a paywall is blurry. For me, the paywall begins when we stop asking questions and sharing general information about the app — and start talking about **plans and trials** .


The beauty of a multi-step paywall is that it lets you break up these moments. It gives each screen a clear purpose instead of overwhelming users with everything at once. That’s why, on average, multi-step paywalls tend to outperform single-screen alternatives.


## The four jobs of a paywall


Paywalls have a hard job: they’re trying to do a *lot* all at once.


1. **Show value:** why is this app for you, and what value does it provide?
2. **Create reassurance and build trust:** reducing the fear of what will happen to your money, and whether it’ll be worth it for you.
3. **Offer choice:** most apps offer multiple options (e.g. monthly/annual or different tiers) — what they all need to do is make the offer clear: the duration and whether there is a trial.
4. **Create enough urgency to convert:** this doesn’t have to be a fake countdown (personally, I’m not a huge fan of those); it just needs to create enough drive to convert now, and show what you’ll miss out on if you don’t.


When you consider all the things your[paywall has to do beyond sell](https://www.revenuecat.com/blog/growth/paywalls-unexpected-uses) , it’s no wonder screens can get crowded and overly complex. But a[simple — even ugly — paywall always wins](https://www.revenuecat.com/blog/growth/ugly-paywalls-conversion-testing/) .


[Hanna Grevelius](https://www.linkedin.com/in/hannagrevelius/) , CPO at Bruce Studios, found this when she worked at fishing app Fishbrain: the simplified paywall (headline, benefits, and payment options) outperformed one where every possible bit of info was included.


Wait. I’m here talking about multi-step paywalls, so why include this single-screen paywall? Because the point is that **simplicity is key** . This paywall manages to say everything it needs to in a single screen, proving that it can be done. If it couldn’t, they’d use multiple steps instead.


In[this case study from Vahe Baghdasaryan](https://www.revenuecat.com/blog/growth/paywall-redesigns-case-studies) , simplifying the paywall for a party game app increased install-to-trial conversion by 31% and revenue by 64%.


Of course, that doesn’t mean a simpler paywall will always win (pretty please, *test it first* ). When the simpler version doesn’t perform as well, the number one reason I see is that a key piece of information was missing, *not* that the added complexity was what made the original work. In those cases, switching to a multi-step paywall outperformed both approaches.


Basically, there’s a difference between:


- Adding pages so you can provide everything the user needs to know and display it clearly
- Adding pages so you can add more information that the user *doesn’t* necessarily need to know


That’s the beauty of multi-step paywalls: they let you include what matters without overwhelming people. Don’t use them as an excuse to cram everything into a few screens. **Use them to communicate what’s important in a way that’s easy to digest.**


## What happens when you split up your paywall


[Mimo](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/mimo-learn-coding-programming/id1133960732) , the coding app, used to have a scrollable paywall.[Ekaterina Gamsriegler](https://www.linkedin.com/in/ekaterina-shpadareva-gamsriegler/) , now Director of Growth at DataCamp, tested breaking it into separate screens. Mimo saw[60% more trial opt-ins](https://mobileuseracquisitionshow.com/episode/monetization-subscriptions-ekaterina-gamsriegler-shpadareva) .


In a separate test, a screen that explained the trial length and promised a cancellation reminder led to “around a 100% increase in the trial opt-in rates” while reducing cancellations in the first 24 hours by 25%. That screen is what’s known as an ‘honest paywall’, an approach popularized by Blinkist (more on that below!): it tells users exactly how the trial works, when they’ll get a reminder, and when they’ll be charged.


Ekaterina also identified it as one of the most impactful changes that[doubled blended lifetime value to customer acquisition cost (LTV:CAC)](https://www.revenuecat.com/blog/growth/optimize-funnel-metrics-mimo) .


That was back in 2022, but looking at a more recent version of Mimo’s paywall, those same principles still appear to be in play.


Screen one focuses on communicating value, showing what users get and featuring reviews. Screen two focuses on building commitment, clearly laying out the price and trial details while promising a cancellation reminder. Together, they help users understand both **what they’re paying for and what they’re signing up for** before making a decision.


### The extra steps usually aren’t about proving value


Looking at multi-step paywalls, much of their strength *isn’t* about convincing users of the value; it’s about building trust. Multi-step paywalls owe a lot to[Blinkist’s honest paywall](https://www.revenuecat.com/blog/growth/how-top-apps-approach-paywalls) , which was only a single screen at the time (and still is).


But it built trust by reducing the number of users who forgot to cancel, or complained post-trial, highlighting that you’ll receive a reminder. For Blinkist, the[results were strong](https://subclub.com/episode/how-ethical-design-led-to-23-growth-jaycee-day-github) :


- **Trial starts:** +23%
- **Complaints:** −55%
- **Push opt-in rate:** 6% → 74%


Multi-step paywalls aim to build that same sense of trust. This is particularly vital as subscription fatigue grows, and more users[cancel their trials on Day 0](https://www.revenuecat.com/blog/growth/post-purchase-screen) ‘just in case’ — with the data showing that 55% of all 3-day trial cancellations happen on Day 0.


Rather than leaving users uncertain, or overwhelming them with too much information at once, apps are increasingly breaking their messaging into smaller, more digestible steps.


Take[Duolingo](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/duolingo-language-lessons/id570060128) , for example. The language-learning app communicates the value of its subscription while letting users choose when they want to receive a trial reminder, giving them a greater sense of control.


As Duolingo’s[Anmol Tiwari](https://www.linkedin.com/in/tiwarianmol/) explained on[Sub Club](https://subclub.com/episode/how-clarity-and-personalization-help-drive-duolingos-growth-anmol-tiwari-duolingo) , this decision to give users a choice helped lift conversion.


[Owen Farmer](https://www.linkedin.com/in/owen-farmer-10275021a/) tested a similar setup for[WordPal, a vocabulary builder app](https://www.revenuecat.com/blog/growth/wordpal-growth-story#unconventional-move-7-not-growing-at-all-costs) , and found a significant lift with the multi-step paywall.


## Testing a multi-step paywall


So how do you work out what to test? Should you use two, three, or four screens? What should you cover on each one? When you start considering all the possibilities, you could fill your backlog with paywall combinations for the next year. But don’t worry, that’s most definitely *not* what I’m recommending.


It’s not about hitting a magic number of screens or trying to cover all four jobs I mentioned earlier:


- Show value
- Create reassurance and build trust
- Offer choice
- Create enough urgency to convert


It’s about identifying the[most important job-to-be-done (JTBD)](https://www.revenuecat.com/blog/growth/jtbd-paywall-optimization/) and working out what stage they’re at in that journey.


The jobs you choose should determine how many screens you need, not the other way around. Most multi-step paywalls have between two and four screens. The final screen typically presents the payment options and clearly explains the terms, while the preceding screens focus on communicating value and reassuring users about the offer.


## Three multi-step paywall patterns to test


Even when you know which jobs your paywall needs to do, it can be hard to know where to start. The combinations and possible setups can feel endless. And while I’d love to believe you’ll take my advice to heart when I say, “Please don’t copy your competitors; find what works best for you”, the reality is that this is *much easier said than done* . Faced with so many options, it’s easy to feel overwhelmed and end up choosing a setup that performs poorly. Trust me, I’ve been there.


So let’s get practical and walk through three common patterns for multi-step paywalls. I asked[Sylvain Gauchet](https://www.linkedin.com/in/sylvaingauchet/) , Head of Growth at Reading.com and creator of[Growth Gems](https://growthgems.co/) , for his best examples of multi-step paywalls, and he highlighted three patterns he sees regularly. He even shared 12 example paywalls, grouped into those three patterns:


What sets those three patterns apart is the **specific doubt they address before asking users to pay** :


1. **Trial reassurance stack: “Will I get charged by surprise?”** The typical flow is a ‘Free trial’ screen → a ‘We’ll remind you’ screen → plan selection and checkout. Each screen is designed to remove a specific fear around signing up.
2. **Lead with value: “Is this worth it for me?”** The flow typically goes from a value-focused screen → a[trial timeline](https://www.revenuecat.com/blog/growth/rip-toggle-paywall) → plan selection, although some apps skip the timeline. The goal is to show users what they’ll gain before asking them to commit.
3. **Risk remover: “What if it doesn’t work for me?”** These paywalls tackle the risk of the app not meeting users’ needs first, then let them customize their trial and decide how much they want to commit.


Let’s look at each pattern in more detail, along with some of the great examples Sylvain kindly shared for each one.


### 1. Trial reassurance stack: “Will I get charged by surprise?”


We’ve already seen examples of this with Duolingo and WordPal, where you can choose when to receive a notification of your trial.


Another great example is[BePresent](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/bepresent-screen-time-control/id1644737181) , a screen-blocking app.


Its structure is similar to WordPal’s (a short text screen, then a reminder), but it adds a second choice: a paid 30-day trial or a free 7-day trial.


Interestingly, the 30-day paid trial is an introductory offer rather than a monthly plan, as the only subscription option available is annual. Giving users a sense of control is a recurring pattern in multi-step paywalls, whether that’s choosing a[trial length](https://www.revenuecat.com/blog/growth/7-day-trial-subscription-app) or selecting a[plan.So](http://plan.so/) offering two different trial formats could therefore be a great experiment to test when you only offer one subscription duration.


### 2. Lead with value: “Is this worth it for me?”


Sylvain shared that the best example of this is[Speak](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/speak-language-learning/id1286609883) , the AI language learning app.


They do a great job of leading with value and outcome you want to achieve, as well as walking through the features in the app. They also reassure you of the trial setup, and that you’ll get an email reminder, before showing a longer paywall that walks through the different plans.


With four plans (Premium vs. Premium Plus and annual vs. monthly) it would have been impossible to fit all of these on one screen. It also shows that you don’t have to choose between short screens and scrollable paywalls; both are possible.


Another good example of this is[Tolan](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/tolan-alien-best-friend/id6477549878) , the AI companion app. They clearly show the value of Tolan Plus — both in terms of offer clarity and an emotional benefit. Meet Karen, my little Tolan (just so I could tell her to “stop being such a Karen”).


Tolan doesn’t lead with a trial but goes straight to plan choice and skips the trial timeline, as the value screens do the work upfront. This also shows how to do this for a[freemium app](https://www.revenuecat.com/blog/growth/freemium-tier-design) effectively: a clear feature comparison to show what premium offers.


Mimo also fits this pattern, but prioritizes only one plan, so it combines the trial timeline and plan option as Blinkist does.


### 3. Risk remover: “What if it doesn’t work for me?”


This style of multi-page paywall lets apps alleviate the fear of whether the app will work for you specifically by leaning less on outcomes and features (as in pattern two), and instead highlighting[money-back or satisfaction guarantees](https://www.revenuecat.com/blog/growth/money-back-guarantee) , social proof, and results or personalized insights.


All with the goal to create confidence that yes, it will work for you.[Reframe](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/reframe-drink-less-thrive/id1485756576) , an app designed to help you reduce drinking, is a strong example of this.


They show your personalized plan, social proof, and publications, as well as the value of what you could save in a year, in terms of calories and better sleep.


It also allows users to customize their trial. One particularly interesting feature worth flagging is the notification toggle, which reassures users that they can opt in to notifications if they choose to. It’s another small but effective way of giving users a sense of control over their experience


[RISE](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/rise-sleep-tracker/id1453884781) , the sleep tracker, has a similar setup. They show you your ideal bedtime and use a guarantee to convince you of the value.


## How to measure your multi-step paywall test in RevenueCat


Your main metric of success should be which paywall delivers higher[average revenue per user (ARPU)](https://www.revenuecat.com/glossary#arpu-average-revenue-per-user) , measured after refunds.


This last bit is important: I once reviewed a paywall experiment that showed a drop in initial conversions and ARPU, with a lower[trial-to-paid conversion rate](https://www.revenuecat.com/glossary#trial-conversion-rate) . They’d added a step that provided more clarity about how the trial worked, and at first glance, it looked like a failed experiment. But when I looked at refunds, they’d dropped from 6% to ~1%, meaning that — after refunds — the variant performed better than the original paywall. Even before considering the negative impact of refunds.


In[RevenueCat Experiments](https://www.revenuecat.com/docs/tools/experiments-v1/experiments-results-v1) , the best way to measure this is realized LTV per customer, which RevenueCat recommends as the main success metric. You can then see refunded customers for each variant next to it.


Illustrative example and data for a single-page vs. multi-page test


Other metrics worth looking at, and where to find them:


- **Paywall view rate** : sometimes you see an improvement in conversion rate, but fewer people are making it to the paywall. Compare paywall viewers in RevenueCat with installs from your analytics or attribution tool.
- **Paywall conversion rate** : how many are converting once they reach the page. RevenueCat’s[paywall conversion chart](https://www.revenuecat.com/docs/dashboard-and-metrics/charts/paywall-conversion-chart) shows this for the screen where you offer your products.
- **Day 0 cancellations** : if you are running a trial, this is a helpful signal of the quality of users. The[trial cancellation rate chart](https://www.revenuecat.com/docs/dashboard-and-metrics/charts/trial-cancellation-chart) lets you look at cancellations within a day of the trial starting.
- **Overall install-to-paid rate** : break it down by trial starts and trial-to-paid conversion rate to work out where and why it has changed.[RevenueCat Experiments](https://www.revenuecat.com/docs/tools/experiments-v1/experiments-results-v1) shows trials started, trial conversion, and conversion to paying for each variant.
- **Division of plans** : sometimes overall conversion rate drops, but you are attracting more longer-term users.[Segment your charts by product](https://www.revenuecat.com/docs/dashboard-and-metrics/charts) to see the split.
- **Drop-off per step** : to work out where people are dropping off in the journey. RevenueCat doesn’t show step-by-step conversion for multi-step paywalls yet, so you’ll need your analytics tool for this.


One thing to check before you start if you build it with RevenueCat: people on[older versions of your app](https://www.revenuecat.com/docs/tools/paywalls#multi-step-paywalls) only see the final screen. Check how many of your users are on an app version with the minimum SDK version for multi-step paywalls; otherwise, part of your variant will see a single-screen paywall and blur the result. You can also set up a[fallback paywall by SDK version](https://www.revenuecat.com/docs/tools/targeting/fallback-paywalls-by-sdk-version) to control what users on older versions see.


## When a multi-step paywall backfires


[Clearful](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/clearful-journal-diary/id1513257639) , a journaling app, was also convinced by multi-step paywalls. They[tested a Blinkist-style timeline page against a long-form page](https://jeffreybunn.substack.com/p/free-trial-timeline-vs-long-form-pricing-page) and got +54% trial starts, yet the retention was worse across every user in the test. After that, they tested the timeline at the top of the long-form page and found that it worked better.


Their hypothesis was that even with multiple screens, they weren't able to communicate the same level of social proof (e.g. testimonials, app features, ratings) and clarity of offering (features and benefits, FAQs) compared to their (very) long-form paywall. It just shows that multi-step isn’t for everyone.


I checked Clearful and they are still using that long-form paywall. They have a multitude of clear (no pun intended) benefit screens before showing a[scrollable paywall](https://www.revenuecat.com/blog/growth/weird-paywalls-drive-subscription-growth) .


[Headspace](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/headspace-sleep-meditation/id493145008) , the meditation app,[tested shortening onboarding, and lengthening it](https://subclub.com/episode/how-headspace-optimized-revenue-by-gating-content-shreya-oswal-and-keya-patel-headspace) , to adjust what they showed before the paywall. However, both[onboarding length variants](https://www.revenuecat.com/blog/growth/everlove-onboarding-experiment) lost to the original middle ground.


Before ruling it out after one failed test, I’d try to understand why it didn’t work. Where did users drop off? What changed in their behavior? Use those insights to inform further tests and experiment with different variations.


As I mentioned at the beginning, the line between onboarding and paywalls is blurring. It follows that **what happens during onboarding can directly impact how users respond to a multi-step paywall** . If you’re simply repeating information or frustrating users with too many questions and too much information during onboarding, adding more screens to the journey isn’t going to help.


But you shouldn’t rule out the approach based on a single test. It takes multiple experiments and a closer analysis of user behavior to understand why something failed before deciding whether it’s worth abandoning altogether.


## Multi-step paywalls for the win?


It’s tempting to assume that shorter paywalls are always better. But when you try to cram everything into fewer screens, you can end up with a worse paywall experience. Think of it like an authentic Italian pizza: a few simple, well-chosen ingredients will always beat 20 different toppings fighting for attention.


I genuinely believe the number of screens is far less important than the cognitive load they create and how the experience feels from start to finish. By breaking information down and sharing it one screen at a time, you can guide users through the journey, helping them understand what your app does and how it can help them. When you give users a sense of choice and control along the way, as many of the examples we’ve explored do, the experience becomes even more effective.


So if your paywall is starting to feel like a pizza with 20 toppings, ask yourself:


1. Which of these toppings (paywall components) are actually adding something to the experience?
2. How can I split them out in a logical way rather than keep them all on one pizza (paywall screen)?


I confess, my analogy gets a bit weaker by the second question, but who doesn’t like having multiple pizzas to choose from rather than just one loaded one?
